Nobody had invited them. They had simply come along, curled up and sleeping, in the clay pot of curry leaves that Murugesan carried across the universe. When he set the pot down on the green planet near Betelgeuse and tipped the old soil from Thanjavur into the red-lit grass, forty-one earthworms tumbled out into a world that had never seen a worm before.

The eldest of them was a thick, slow, wise old worm whom the others called Periyamma. She lifted her front end, tasted the air, and felt the warm soil under her belly.

"This earth is soft," she said. "This earth is hungry. We will stay."

The aliens found them on the ninety-first day. They were called the Thoovals, though the worms only learned that much later. They were tall and soft-footed, with skin the colour of young banana leaves, four long fingers on each hand, and wide amber eyes that blinked sideways. They farmed in a clumsy, patient way, scratching at the hard ground with stone sticks and losing half of every crop to the dry crust.

A young Thooval named Ilavi knelt by the river and saw a worm come up out of the loosened earth. She did not scream. She did not step on it. She put her long finger down, very gently, and the worm — a bold young one called Kuttan — climbed on.

"Who are you," Ilavi said, in a voice like wind through reeds, "and why is the ground here so alive?"

That night Kuttan dreamed of the hard grey crust of the Thooval fields and woke up delighted. The Thoovals had started calling the worms "the breath of the ground", and the Thooval children said it like a blessing every morning. Ilavi knelt beside Selvi and asked, in a voice like reeds, how soil could be made so soft. On the night of the first Harvest Festival, the Thoovals lit a hundred small lamps along the edges of the fields, and the worms came up to the surface to feel the warm light on their skin. Ilavi, older now, sat beside the furrow where she had first met Kuttan. Children of both peoples played in the soft earth: Thooval little ones with mud to their elbows, tiny worm-children wriggling between their toes.

Periyamma was very old by then. She came up slowly, rested her head on a fallen silver leaf, and looked at the lamps and the tall grain and the great red star sinking behind the hills.

"In the place we came from," she said, "there was a saying. A man named Valluvar said that the world turns behind the plough, and everyone else only follows. We are small, and we have no hands and no eyes. But we turned the soil. And look what grew."

Ilavi bent down, put out one long finger, and Periyamma, for the first and only time, climbed on.

Above them, in a sky the colour of kumkum, the stars came out one by one, and the soil of Pudhu Mann breathed softly in the dark.
